Service report helpfully defines privatization as “the use of the private 
sector in the provision of a good or service, the components of which include 
financing, operations (supplying, production, delivery), and quality 
control.” Ke v in R. Ko s a r , Co n g . Re s e a r c h Se r v ., RL 33777, 
Pr iv a t iz a t io n a n d t h e Fe d e r a l  Go v e r n me n t : An In t r o d u c t io n 3 
(2006). It may take a variety of forms, including “divestiture/load-shedding, 
contracting for goods, contracting for services (outsourcing), vouchers, 
quasi-governmental entities (including government-owned contractor- 
operated facilities (GOCO)), third-party financing, grants to private 
parties, prize competitions, and the use of volunteers.” Id. at 12-13.
The privatization phenomenon means that the number of contractors 
and grantees who effectively work for the federal government greatly 
outnumbers the ranks of federal civil servants. The scholar who has 
studied the issue most exhaustively finds the ratio of contract and grant 
employees to federal employees has been relatively stable at between 2.2 
and 2.6 to 1 between 1984 and 2015, with temporary surges in the first 
decade of the twenty-first century. Grant and contract employees, that is, 
“surged from 2002 to 2005 as US troops, defense contract employees, and a 
small number of grant employees were sent to Iraq and Afghanistan [and] 
surged again after Obama launched his $830 billion grant-filled stimulus 
plan in 2009.” PAUL C. LIGHT, THE TRUE SIZE OF GOVERNMENT: TRACKING 
Wa s h in g t o n ’s Bl e n d e d  Wo r k f o r c e , 1984-2015, at 4-5 (Volcker Alliance 
2017).
The purported benefits of privatization include greater efficiency and 
flexibility in the performance of public services, plus increased economic 
stimulus for the private sector. But, of course, a major source of enhanced 
flexibihty is the fact that private actors go unregulated by laws such as the 
Administrative Procedure Act and Freedom of Information Act, which 
impose significant requirements on government agencies in order to help 
assure accountabihty and transparency. As the 2006 CRS report states:
* * * [I]n shifting an activity from the governmental to the private 
sector, the nature of government oversight is transformed. As the 
components of government provision of goods and services are 
privatized, the jurisdiction of federal management laws. 
Congress, the President, and the courts is reduced.
Moreover, privatization shifts government administrative 
management from implementation to oversight as hierarchical 
oversight may be replaced by contractual relationships. 
Government oversight of privatized government activities, or 
“third party government,” on a large scale is a recent phenomenon 
and one that many federal administrators and public 
administration scholars have found vexatious.
